ideas.name: three-tine comb pad
ideas.description: A printed PLA pad carrying three TPU-skinned grooved tines, 8 mm wide, at -20, 0 and +20 mm along the jaw width. Its vertical profile is the same as the current pad (reach 3 mm, tilt 8.8 deg, groove 6 mm). The centre tine keeps the current contact for small objects. On a long object the outer tines add 40 mm of contact spacing, which resists twisting about the closing axis.
ideas.test: Add a pads variant to the simulator with three separate contact boxes per face at the given offsets, with the current profile geometry. Then rerun mustard_bottle, dice, golf_ball and tomato_soup_can.

ideas.name: 12 V gripper servo only
ideas.description: Replace only the gripper's STS3215 (7.4 V, 1.62 N*m) with an STS3215 12 V (2.94 N*m), powered from a separate 12 V supply. Its power lead is split from the 7.4 V bus while it shares the TTL data line with the other five servos. The rack-and-pinion jaw and pads are unchanged, so the squeeze rises from about 27 N to about 49 N at every opening. Per-object force can be capped through the servo's torque-limit register.
ideas.test: The simulator needs an arm_servos variant that gives the gripper joint alone 2.94 N*m stall while the lifting joints stay at 1.62 N*m, plus a per-task force cap that System 1 can tune.

proposals.edit: jaw -> prismatic (drive_mm_per_rad=58)
proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (pudding, sugar, mustard, tuna, both placements each) and squeezed_down_out from a tilted moving face (gelatin, apple, potted meat, screwdriver). On the hinge, the moving face is parallel at one opening only, and its fingertip rises as it opens. The brief gives +14 mm and 44 deg at 75 mm, +23 mm and 53 deg at 85 mm, and +35 mm and 64 deg at 95 mm. The low boxes have their top only 15–29 mm above centre, so the rising tip lands on the top face: the logs show contacts at +19/+19, +20/+23, +22/+29 and +14/+17 pushing 83–88 deg down. Gelatin (contact at +10 mm, 49 deg down), apple (29–36 deg down) and potted meat (24 deg down) are squeezed out by the tilt.
proposals.principle: Two contacts hold only when their normals are horizontal and opposed. A face that turns with its joint is parallel at one opening only, and a swinging fingertip rises by about R(1−cos q). The finger must reach below the object's top to hold its side.
proposals.hypothesis:
No value in the stock parts fixes this. The revolute jaw has no parameters, and the tilt and rise are tied to the opening. Pads at 45 deg still leave +14 deg and +14 mm at 85 mm. The parallelogram keeps the face parallel but still lets the tip rise +33 mm at 85 mm (link 90), which is the same top-face failure. The prismatic jaw is the only catalogue part with 0 deg and +1 mm at every width.

I set drive_mm_per_rad to 58. Opening grows roughly linearly from 51 mm at 20 to 121 mm at 60, so 58 gives about 117 mm. That fits the 96 mm mustard bottle and 92 mm sugar box with side clearance, and the squeeze is about 1.62/0.058 ≈ 28 N.

Friction check (2μN against weight): sugar 2·0.5·28 = 28 N vs 5.0 N; mustard 22 N vs 4.2 N; potted meat 2·0.35·28 = 19.6 N vs 3.6 N. Arm load for the 514 g sugar box: 0.41 + 0.77 = 1.18 N·m, under the 1.62 N·m stall, leaving about 0.4 N·m for the added slide mass.

Bill of materials: lm3uu_bearing ×2 ($2.40), steel_rod_3x100 ×2 ($3.00), m3 screws on hand, PLA 32 g (160 machine min). Total $5.40, 3 days. It fits the $40, 7-day and 600-min limits.
risks: golf_ball, lemon, plum, strawberry, racquetball, tennis_ball, tomato_soup_can: these roll. Flat parallel faces don't centre a sphere; they hold it only at its equator. The fingertip no longer rises (+1 mm), so System 1 can set the grasp height at the equator. The current hinge pushes these objects off-axis and they are held anyway, so horizontal normals should be no worse.

dice (17 mm) and large_marker (19 mm): at 58 mm/rad, 2 mm of opening is about 0.035 rad of servo travel, which is fine-grained enough for the close target. The squeeze (28 N) is higher than today's 20 N.
banana and cup: parallel faces at 57–70 mm replace the 36–44 deg tilt, and the stronger squeeze should be harmless for a 13 g cup. If the cup crushes, the parameter fit can move drive toward 60.

proposals.edit: pads -> pads (groove_mm=2, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=20, pad_tpu_mm=1.5, reach_mm=0, width_mm=12)
proposals.mechanism: squeezed_down_out at moderate tilt: apple (moving jaw 29–36 deg down), potted meat (24 deg down) and screwdriver (7–11 deg down) slip under the tilted moving face on the stock hinge.
proposals.principle: A tilted contact pushes the object down with N·sin(a), and friction μN must resist it. The holding condition is roughly tan(a) < μ. TPU raises μ from 0.45 to 0.9, and tilting the pad back moves the parallel opening toward the mid-range widths.
proposals.hypothesis:
This is the cheap fallback if the slide doesn't help. It costs $0, takes 0 days and 16 machine min, and acts on the pads slot only, so it can be combined with the jaw swap. A pad angle of 20 deg puts the moving face near parallel around 45–60 mm, where the failing apple and potted meat contacts sit. The brief gives about +20 deg at 35 mm for angle 0 and −8 deg at 55 mm for angle 45, so 20 deg lands roughly at parallel for mid-range widths. TPU then gives tan(a) < 0.9 for tilts up to about 42 deg.

It cannot fix the top-face cases. Tip rise is +14 mm at 85 mm even at 45 deg, so the boxes stay with the jaw swap.
risks: dice, large_marker and wood_block_cube: the 20 deg back-tilt makes the moving face lean the other way at 17–26 mm, roughly −10 deg with the bottom swung in. That would pinch the cubes upward rather than squeeze them out, and the TPU friction margin should absorb it.

tomato_soup_can (349 g) and tennis_ball (66 mm): the face is about 6–8 deg further from parallel at these widths than the 36 deg it shows today. The higher TPU friction (tan 44 deg is about 0.97, which is near μ = 0.9) makes this borderline, and the trial will decide.

proposals.mechanism: squeezed_down_out: both pads touch the lying mustard bottle above its equator. The fixed-jaw contact is +8 mm and the moving-jaw contact +9 to +10 mm from the centre (top at +29), so the contact normals push 7–14 deg down. The 25 N squeeze drives the bottle down and out of the jaws (it ended at +24 mm and at -2 mm).
proposals.principle: A round object is held at its equator: contacts above it push it down. reach_mm extends both pads below the stock fingertips, which moves the contact band down by the same amount at a fixed wrist height. With the contacts at the equator the normals become horizontal and antipodal, and the squeeze stops pushing the bottle out.
proposals.hypothesis: Keep the current jaw (prismatic, 60 mm/rad, 27 N, tip offset +1 mm at every opening) and every pad value that holds the dice: pad_angle 8.8, TPU 1.31, groove 3.34. Only add reach_mm of about 9 mm to match the measured 8–10 mm contact offset. b00t0 had reach 8.6 and gained mustard_bottle. It lost dice, but b001 had reach 0 and lost dice too. Both had pad_angle 0, so the dice loss tracks the angle, not the reach. No other slot can fix this. The jaw already gives parallel, non-rising faces. The squeeze has margin: 2*0.4*25 = 20 N against 4.2 N of weight. The 12 V servos are over budget and are not needed anyway: 431 g needs 0.41+0.65 = 1.06 N*m against 1.62 N*m. Cost: reprinting the pads (2 g PLA + 1 g TPU, about 18 machine min, $0).
risks: dice / large_marker / wood_block_cube: longer pads with an 8.8 deg tilt bring the moving tip about 1.4 mm further inward at the bottom. This should survive because the tilt that holds the dice now is unchanged and System 1 retunes the close target.

gelatin_box, flat_screwdriver, banana (low objects): the pads now hang 9 mm lower, so the wrist must stay higher to clear the table. System 1 tunes the grasp height through side and lift, so this should survive.
tomato_soup_can, golf_ball and other rolling objects: their contacts also move down toward or below their equators. Each object's grasp height is tuned separately, so this should survive.

Both are the cheapest move up the ladder: a params change, $0 to buy, about 18 machine min to reprint the pads, which uses parts already on hand. iterations.notes:
I sent three proposals for the one failing group, the mustard bottle. All are cheap parameter changes: no purchases and almost no print time.

**Diagnosis:** The bottle (96 mm across, 431 g, friction 0.4) is gripped about 5 mm above its middle, so both jaws push it slightly downward. It lifted 26 mm, then slid back to +18 mm while held: a slow slip, not a drop. On paper the grip should hold, so the fix is more margin, not a new part.

**Why not a bigger change:**
- **Longer pads:** five pad-only trials show that making them longer to grip lower costs the dice or the potted meat can.
- **12 V servos:** refused, since they cost $68 and $34.60 is left. They would only add lifting torque at the shoulder, elbow and wrist anyway, not grip.
- **Lip at the pad bottom:** skipped. It sits at the same height as the fingertip, still above the bottle's middle, so it wouldn't lower the grip, and the two lips could hit each other when closing on the dice.

**The three proposals:**
1. **Jaw drive 60 → 56 mm/rad.** Squeeze rises from 27 N to about 28.9 N. By my estimate from the brief's figures, the maximum opening falls to about 104 mm, still about 4 mm per side for the 92–96 mm objects. The main risk is that tighter clearance on the wide boxes.
2. **Pads 9.5 → 16 mm wide, nothing else changed.** A longer contact along the bottle should resist it twisting and creeping down. It keeps the tilt and length settings the dice depends on.
3. **Pads 3 → 4 mm longer.** This is the untried step between 3 mm (kept) and 5 mm (lost the dice), so it is the riskiest of the three for the dice.

The jaw and pad changes are in different slots, so if 1 is kept along with 2 or 3, they will also be tried together.

proposals.mechanism: slipped_under_load on reg_mustard_bottle: both pads touch at +5 mm above the bottle's equator (top at +29), so the contact normals push it 2 deg (fixed) and 4 deg (moving) down. The pad bottom edges sit on the upper flank, and the bottle slides from +42 mm to +25 mm during the hold. Friction capacity (2*0.4*26 = 20.8 N against 4.2 N weight) and arm torque (about 1.06 of 1.62 N*m) are not the limits.
proposals.principle: A round or convex object is held at its equator: contacts above it push it down and squeeze it out. Lowering the contact toward the equator turns the normals horizontal (antipodal).
proposals.hypothesis: The record shows reach is the lever that lowers the contact: b00t0 (reach 8.6) held the mustard, and b001 (reach 0) did not. Reach of 4 mm or more loses the dice, but 3.5 has never been tried. A 0.5 mm deeper pad brings the contact from +5 toward +4.5 mm and reduces the down component by about 10%. The best score is 0.50 and the bottle ends only about 5 mm short, so a small margin may be enough. Cheaper moves are exhausted: tilt, TPU, groove and width have all been run to their limits in the record.
risks: dice: every reach of 4 mm or more lost it (squeezed out with the fingertips closing past it). 3.5 is half the step to that boundary, so it is the most likely loss.
Small objects held near the fingertip (large_marker, wood_block_cube) could shift slightly. The pad tilt and squeeze are unchanged, so they should hold.
proposals.result: KEPT: gained mustard_bottle, lost none; costs $0.00, 11 machine min

proposals.edit: pads (groove_mm=6, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=8.798, pad_tpu_mm=2, reach_mm=3.5, width_mm=19)
proposals.mechanism: slipped_under_load on reg_mustard_bottle (contact 5 mm above the equator, pushing 2-4 deg down; the bottle also tends to pitch about the jaw axis because the 191 mm long bottle is gripped off its centre of mass).
proposals.principle: Friction holds the load only with margin. A longer contact patch along the bottle adds resisting moment against pitching, and a lower contact removes the downward squeeze-out component.
proposals.hypothesis: Widening the pads from 16 to 18 mm, together with the 6 mm groove, gained a mustard placement with no loss. 21 and 24 mm overshot onto the bottle's taper (squeezed_down_out). 19 mm is the untried step inside that window, and pairing it with reach 3.5 lowers the contact at the same time. Each lever alone is a half-step, so the body stays close to the kept one.
risks: dice: reach 3.5 is the same risk as in proposal 1.
mustard's other placement: width 21 pushed the bottle out downward (squeezed_down_out). 19 is closer to the kept 18, so it should stay clear of the taper.
Wide boxes (sugar_box, pudding_box) were unaffected by width changes in past trials.
proposals.result: not kept (another proposal gained more): gained mustard_bottle, lost none; costs $0.00, 12 machine min

proposals.mechanism: slipped_under_load on reg_mustard_bottle: 26 N per jaw is marginal against the heaviest long object's pitch and slide once the contact sits above the equator. Squeeze on the slide is fixed at servo torque / pinion radius (1.62/0.06 = 27 N). The pinion cannot get smaller without losing the 96 mm opening (drive 58 already lost tomato_soup_can), and the catalogue's 12 V option costs $68 against the $34.60 left.
proposals.principle: Squeeze is servo torque over the pinion radius. Friction capacity and frictional resisting moment both scale with squeeze, so raising torque alone keeps the opening and multiplies the holding margin.
proposals.hypothesis: Only the gripper servo needs more torque: the arm uses 1.06 of 1.62 N*m with the bottle. One 12 V STS3215 on the gripper on its own 12 V supply gives 2.94 N*m, so about 49 N per jaw on the same 60 mm/rad slide and 110 mm opening. Its torque-limit register lets the controller keep today's force on objects that are sensitive to squeeze (tomato_soup_can).
risks: tomato_soup_can: the higher squeeze from drive 58 lost it, so the servo's torque limit must be tunable per object.
dice and small round objects: more force with a tilted pad could squeeze them out. Mitigated by the same torque cap.

idea.name: 12 V gripper servo only
idea.description: Replace only the gripper's STS3215 (7.4 V, 1.62 N*m) with an STS3215 12 V (2.94 N*m), powered from a separate 12 V supply. Its power lead is split from the 7.4 V bus while it shares the TTL data line with the other five servos. The rack-and-pinion jaw and pads are unchanged, so the squeeze rises from about 27 N to about 49 N at every opening. Per-object force can be capped through the servo's torque-limit register.
idea.test: The simulator needs an arm_servos variant that gives the gripper joint alone 2.94 N*m stall while the lifting joints stay at 1.62 N*m, plus a per-task force cap that System 1 can tune.

proposals.result: idea recorded, not tested: 12 V gripper servo only; it would need $32.00 from the manifest, 5 days, 0 machine min; within the budget left

iterations.notes: Pad and jaw parameters are close to exhausted for the mustard bottle. The dice limits reach (below 4 mm) and tilt (no lower than 8.8 deg), the taper limits width (below 21 mm), and squeeze changes lose the tomato soup can. Proposals 1-2 are the last untried half-steps that lower the contact. Proposal 3 is the one affordable way to add squeeze ($32, 5 days) without giving up the opening.
